name: Alipilus (Roman plucker slave)

lead: In ancient Rome, smooth skin was linked with status and refinement, and enslaved attendants called alipili removed unwanted hair for bathers. Underarm plucking is the task most associated with the role.
The appearance payoff was a hairless, groomed look at the bath and in public. Evidence comes mainly from classical and later historical accounts, summarized in general histories of hair removal.

paras: Historically, a household or bath attendant plucked hair by hand or with tools, and depilatory preparations such as psilothrum and dropax were also used. Women were served by female attendants.
Plucking is painful and can irritate skin. The role itself was part of the institution of slavery, which is how it is described in historical accounts.

angle.text: Plucking by an attendant left the underarms hairless, producing the smooth appearance Romans associated with refinement. Today the same goal is pursued with razors, waxing, laser and similar methods.

lead: An alipilus (plural alipili) was an enslaved attendant in ancient Rome whose job was removing unwanted body hair for clients, most famously by plucking underarm hair.[1]

Hair removal in Rome carried social meaning: smooth skin was associated with purity and superiority, and both men and women removed body hair.[1] The alipilus was one way wealthier households and bathers obtained a groomed look without doing it themselves.[1]
infobox: Plucking and removal of body hair

paras: Enslaved attendants called alipili removed unwanted hair for bathers, and female attendants served women.[1] Romans also used depilatory preparations such as psilothrum and dropax.[1]
Smooth skin signalled status in Roman culture; the emperor Augustus is reported by Suetonius to have used heated nutshells on his legs for depilation.[1]
